title: v6 batch: 24 plans and 96 builds, Nov 3–4
summary:
I went through all 120 runs of prompt v6 (Nov 3, 17:47 to Nov 4, 10:55): 24 plans by Opus 5.5 at max effort, each built four times, by Opus xhigh, Opus medium, Sonnet medium and Haiku medium. I read the goal checks in every transcript. Three helper agents read and tagged all 1,344 exit-interview answers, and a fourth read the 24 planners' replies. I spot-checked their counts against the raw answers. I also loaded all 96 games in headless Chromium. Nothing real was run: the dashboard and runner changes were tested in sandboxes with the fake CLIs, and `runs/` is as it was.

What we learned, in short:

1. **The goal check decided the outcome more than the models did.** 73 of 96 builds never passed it, and Claude Code stopped 64 of them after 9 blocked stops. The last checks mostly asked for things this computer can't show (a real pad, sound heard, a person playing) or for proof the agent's own tests couldn't give, and TASK.md forbade asking anyone else. $544 (22%) of the build spend came after a builder first tried to stop. #22 changed the goal and added the machine file after this batch started, so the next batch is the test of that fix (GOAL-1 to GOAL-3).

2. **The plan is the next lever.**
   - Every builder said the plan is too big, and 77 asked for a must/should/could ranking (PLAN-1).
   - 23 of 25 plans write the plan run's own file names, which 67 builders had to translate (PLAN-2).
   - The title rule pulls two ways: 10 builds re-drew the title, and 2 that kept the plan's were marked down for it (PLAN-3).

3. **Opus xhigh is the builder that finishes.**
   - It met the goal 13 times, against 8 for Opus medium, 2 for Sonnet and 0 for Haiku.
   - It costs $96 per goal met, the lowest of the four (Opus medium $115, Sonnet $138).
   - Haiku stopped after 29 minutes (median) and openly cut features (MODEL-1 to MODEL-3).

| | Opus xhigh | Opus medium | Sonnet medium | Haiku medium |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Goal met | 13 of 24 | 8 of 24 | 2 of 24 | 0 of 24 |
| Stopped by Claude Code | 7 | 15 | 22 | 20, and 4 timed out |
| First tried to stop (median) | 124 min | 75 min | 41 min | 29 min |
| Time (median) | 162 min | 110 min | 56 min | 56 min |
| Cost (median / total) | $54 / $1,253 | $38 / $919 | $10 / $275 | $6 / $147 |
| Cost per goal met | $96 | $115 | $138 | none met |
| Issues its own testing found (median) | 33 | 25 | 10 | 12 |
| Changed the engine | 24 | 24 | 19 | 11 |
| Drew its own title | 1 | 2 | 0 | 7 |
| Game size (median) | 1,746 KB | 1,641 KB | 1,467 KB | 1,425 KB |
| Attract demo starts on its own (within 2 min) | 24 | 24 | 23 (1 throws on every frame) | 23 (1 throws on every frame) |
| No touch-only notice | 0 | 0 | 2 | 3 |

4. **Run data had a hole.** None of the 64 builds Claude Code stopped kept its final reply: the CLI's result was empty, though the answer was in the output. The runner now reads it, and `--reparse` fills the 64 in. That rewrites committed run data, so the permission check stopped me, and it's your call (DATA-1).

5. **The computer was under strain.**
   - All 24 planners filled /tmp, which is held in memory, by downloading the engine and hub repos into it at the same time. 6.4 GB of older agent leftovers are still there.
   - 33 test servers that agents started are still running (ENV-1, ENV-2).

6. **The games mostly hold up when loaded cold.** All 96 load headless without an error. Two attract modes throw on every frame, and 5 games skip the touch-only notice, though their builders' tests passed (GAME-1).

The Insights tab gained **What the agents said**, which shows every answer to one question across the runs in view, by model, with a search. It also has a check that the builds of one plan keep its title. Engine feedback for the my-3D2dge repo is under Engine.

decisions.title: Fill in the 64 missing replies: `node run-matrix.mjs --reparse` (DATA-1)
decisions.detail: The runner fix only helps new runs. Run this once in the repo folder to give the 64 builds Claude Code stopped their `reply.md`. It also sets their `replyChars` and adds the reply to their game's record. I tried it on a sandbox copy first. Those were the only changes: other result.json files stayed the same, and no other game was rewritten (DATA-2). The permission check blocked me from running it on the committed run data, which is the right call for an agent, so it's yours.

decisions.title: Rank the plan (PLAN-1)
decisions.detail: Add one line to the plan stage's Instructions, for example: "Mark every feature must, should or could, and say what to cut first if time runs short." All 96 builders raised scope somewhere, and this was the most common request (77). It also gives the goal check something to measure "done" against. Optional: ask for a smaller first milestone that is a complete game.

decisions.title: Settle the game's title (PLAN-3)
decisions.detail: TASK.md's Game Title tells every builder to draw a title at random. The plan has already drawn one. Pick one rule. Either the build stage says "Use PLAN.md's title", or the Game Title variant says the planner picks it. Insights now checks this: Expectations → Builds of one plan use its title (8 of 25 plans fail it today).

decisions.title: Keep file names out of PLAN.md (PLAN-2)
decisions.detail: Add to the plan stage: "Don't write file or folder names: each builder takes its own from its TASK.md." 23 of 25 plans hard-coded the planner's names, like `SnipeoutHD-WipeoutHD-claude-opus-5-5-max-20261103-174728.html`. 67 builders said translating them cost time. No build shipped under a wrong name.

decisions.title: Decide whether a builder may ask for an outside review (GOAL-3)
decisions.detail: The Testing variant says "Don't use subagents or workflows to debate, review, judge or audit". The goal check kept saying the agent's own tests and checklists weren't independent evidence, and several builders stopped there. Watch the next batch's goal reasons (Results → details, or Insights → Needs a look). If it comes up again, either allow one review subagent at the end, or say in the goal that the agent's own tests count.

decisions.title: Haiku's place in the build stage (MODEL-1)
decisions.detail: Haiku met none of its 24 goals. It first tried to stop after a median of 29 minutes on plans of about 140 KB. 4 of its runs hit the 120-minute limit, which is 180 now. It re-drew 7 of the 10 changed titles. Its cost was small ($147 for all 24). Options: drop it from the build stage; give it a smaller plan, such as the must-haves only once PLAN-1 is in; or keep it as the floor and expect partial games.

decisions.title: Clean up /tmp and the leftover servers (ENV-1, ENV-2)
decisions.detail: /tmp is held in memory, and 6.4 GB in it is old agent work. The biggest folder is `/tmp/bb-xb81546` (5.4 GB, from the Nov 2 Breaking Bad runs); the others are `/tmp/x22cc1b-dl`, `/tmp/s55eng`, `/tmp/mm-research-xe8b2f0`, `/tmp/x3ec78e`, `/tmp/s55` and `/tmp/x96eb17`. 33 `python3 -m http.server` processes from runs are still listening. ENV-2 has the commands. Longer term, the runner could give each run its own `TMPDIR` inside its folder, so tools that write temp files can't fill the shared /tmp.

decisions.title: Load each finished game once, headless (GAME-1)
decisions.detail: The audit's smoke test found 2 attract modes that throw on every frame, 2 that never start, and 5 games without the touch notice, in builds whose own tests passed. The runner could load each finished game in headless Chromium for about 20 seconds. It would record page and console errors and a screenshot in result.json, and Needs a look would flag a game that throws. It costs about 20 seconds per run, and Playwright is already here.

decisions.title: Drop or automate the Usage line (PROMPT-1)
decisions.detail: 94 of 96 builders wrote "unknown": an agent can't see its own cost. The runner already records the real figures in result.json and the game's record. Either remove Usage from the Source Information variant, or say "the runner fills this in".

findings.title: 73 of 96 builds never passed their goal check; Claude Code stopped 64 of them after 9 blocked stops
findings.found:
Goal met: Opus xhigh 13 of 24, Opus medium 8, Sonnet 2, Haiku 0. All 24 plans passed on the first check. 17 of 24 briefs had at least one build that passed.

The last check of each unmet build said what was missing. I read all 73:

- **Things this computer can't show.** No physical DualSense, no touch device, sound never heard, no human playthrough, no real AI Hub session with people. These come up in most Opus and Sonnet failures. Example: sonnet-medium TimeCrisis3 was checked 48 times in 32 minutes on the same three items: "Real DualSense: there is no physical controller", boss-state replica sync and one death never seen on screen.
- **The agent's own evidence wasn't independent enough** (GOAL-3).
- **Features really missing**, mostly Haiku. For example, haiku-medium WipeoutHD had "only 5 of 10 weapons, 2 of 4 tracks". 4 Haiku runs stopped to ask the user to choose a narrower scope, which nobody can answer in a headless run (densha-de-go, tenchu2, TrackMania and brigandine).
- **Reply format.** 4 Sonnet runs said the sections were "in my previous reply" instead of repeating them.
- **The title** (PLAN-3).
findings.did:
Nothing new here: #22 (merged today, after this batch started) is the fix.

- It changed the build goal to "Everything in PLAN.md that can be done on this computer is done, and everything TASK.md asks you to hand in is in this folder."
- It added `environments/Worki9.md`. That file says what this computer can't test, gives the stand-ins to use, and says anything that needs the real thing "is checked as far as it can be here, never required".

The next batch is the test. Insights → Expectations → "Finished runs meet their /goal" shows the rate.
findings.check: `goalMet`, `goalChecks`, `goalForced` and `goalReason` in all 120 result.json files, and each check read again from the transcripts in `~/.claude/projects` (117 of 120 found; 3 Haiku runs that hit the time limit have none).

findings.title: 64 builds had no final reply: Claude Code's result is empty when it stops a /goal turn itself
findings.found:
When Claude Code overrides the stop hook after 9 blocks, the stream's last `result` line has `"result":""`. The runner took the reply only from that line, so `reply.md` was never written. Results' reply button and the record in each game came up empty for these runs, and Insights flagged them under "no reply" (77 of 488 finished runs).

The answer isn't lost. The agent's last response in `agent.out` holds it. In sonnet-medium TimeCrisis3 it has all four sections. Affected builds: Haiku 20, Sonnet 22, Opus medium 15, Opus xhigh 7. Older forced runs from Nov 3 are affected too.
findings.did: `parseClaude` now falls back to the last response's text when the result is empty (not for an error, and not for a made-up `<synthetic>` message), as `sessionEnd` already did for runs cut off mid-session. `--reparse` now writes `reply.md` for a run that has none and whose output has a reply; a `reply.md` already there is left alone. Running it on the real runs is in Your call.
findings.check: `test/runner.test.mjs` (the /goal test): the fake Claude CLI now ends a forced turn with an empty result like the real one. The reply comes from the last response, and `--reparse` fills in a deleted `reply.md` and leaves one that's there alone. The test fails on the old runner. A sandbox copy of 5 real runs (3 forced) gave the 3 forced runs their reply (1,783 to 4,309 characters) and changed nothing else.

findings.title: Every builder said the plan was bigger than one session, and 77 asked for it to be ranked
findings.found:
The plans run 113 to 201 KB (median 142 KB, about 1,500 to 2,400 lines). They cover 8 to 14 milestones and 10 to 16 risks, with several modes, tracks or chapters each. All 96 builders raised scope somewhere in their prompt feedback: opus-xhigh 3, opus-medium 13, Sonnet 24 and Haiku 21 called it confusing or too big.

Their most common request was "rank the plan must/should/could, with a cut order" (77 runs). Next came a time or token budget (19), a smaller first milestone (18) and a target size for the demo (13).

The "done" bar read as the whole plan in 27 runs. Done and the goal say "every feature … no stubs", and STAGE.md says to follow the plan, so nothing could be left out without counting as a stub. opus-medium american-football: "'follow the plan' versus 'TASK.md wins' and 'no stubbed features' needed judgment about what to cut without leaving stubs".

How long each builder worked before it first tried to stop (median): Haiku 29 minutes, Sonnet 41, Opus medium 75, Opus xhigh 124.
findings.did: Left for you. One line in the plan stage would do it (Your call). It's in keeping with "start simple, add detail only when runs need it": these runs need it.
findings.check: The prompt-feedback catalogue (all 384 answers tagged; every quote checked to be verbatim), PLAN.md sizes from `planChars`, and first-check times from the transcripts.

findings.title: All 24 planners filled /tmp, which is held in memory, and 6.4 GB of older agent work is still in it
findings.found:
/tmp is a 9.8 GB tmpfs, so whatever sits in it uses RAM on a computer with 20 GB.

- **During the batch:** all 24 plan transcripts hit "No space left on device" or Claude Code's "0 MB free" notice, and so did 19 of 93 build transcripts. 22 of 24 planners downloaded the engine and ai-hub repos into /tmp, all starting within about a minute of each other. Three plans lost command output to it. The planners blamed "other agents".
- **Now:** 1.8 GB is free. 6.4 GB is older agent work, mostly `/tmp/bb-xb81546/dl` (5.4 GB, from the Nov 2 Breaking Bad runs). The rest is `/tmp/x22cc1b-dl`, `/tmp/s55eng`, `/tmp/mm-research-xe8b2f0`, `/tmp/x3ec78e`, `/tmp/s55` and `/tmp/x96eb17`, each 150 to 175 MB.
- **During this audit:** a sandbox copy of mine filled it for a moment. I deleted it at once and moved my sandboxes to `~/.cache`.
findings.did: Nothing deleted. #22's machine file now tells agents to keep their files out of /tmp. See Your call for the cleanup and a per-run `TMPDIR`.
findings.check: `df -h /tmp`, `du -sh /tmp/*`, and a search of all 117 transcripts for the full-disk messages and for downloads into /tmp.

findings.title: Builders made the same engine patches up to 55 times over, so they belong in my-3D2dge
findings.found:
78 of 96 builds changed the engine: all 48 Opus builds, 19 Sonnet and 11 Haiku. The same changes were made over and over, each copy on its own:

| Change | Runs |
|---|---|
| PlayStation button symbols by default (the setting defaults to "auto", and a game can't set it) | 55 |
| A public audio bus, so code-made voices follow volume and mute | 39 |
| Font glyphs: the 5×7 pixel font has no ✕ ○ □ △, though `input.label()` returns them, so they print as "?" (55 runs hit this); also missing are the middle dot, dashes, arrows, ticks and accents | 32 |
| A per-letter voice hook in E.Dialog (it plays one sound per page) | 29 |
| A guard so the AI Hub's Create+Options doesn't open the pause menu | 22 |
| Humanoid hats and hair, outfits, weapons | 19, 17, 16 |
| Settings rows on any Shell screen; synth extensions | 11 each |
| Analog triggers; an exported per-step hook | 8 each |

TASK.md requires PlayStation symbols by default, so the first row is a patch every game needs. The plans asked for several of these patches up front.
findings.did: Nothing here: it's for the engine repo. Each run's own patch is in its dev folder, under `runs/<run>/work/<Game>/` (not in git). The Engine Feedback question in Insights → What the agents said has every answer.
findings.check: Engine-feedback catalogue: all 576 answers tagged; every quote checked to be verbatim, and every run key checked to exist. I spot-checked the button-symbol, audio-bus and font counts against the raw answers (61, 37 and 32 mentions).

findings.title: After the first stop attempt, the medium builders mostly just tried to stop again
findings.found:
Most builds that kept going after a failed check didn't do much new work. They mostly ran the tests again and wrote the same message again.

| | Haiku | Sonnet | Opus medium | Opus xhigh |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Re-checks within a minute of the one before | 76% | 83% | 65% | 55% |
| Median gap between checks | 0.1 min | 0.2 min | 0.4 min | 4.6 min |
| Median checks per run | 13 | 21 | 17 | 5 |

Opus xhigh still fixed real problems between checks. For opus-xhigh cricket, the checker notes that "missing music layers, deep-link crashes, dead menu rows, the touch gate" were found late.

Estimated from each response's tokens at list-price ratios, $544 of the $2,523 build spend (22%) came after the builder first tried to stop, and $459 of that was in runs that never passed. That's 46 of 156 agent-hours.
findings.did: Nothing to change on its own. It shrinks when GOAL-1 and GOAL-3 do. Each run's details show its goal checks and the last reason.
findings.check: Goal-check timestamps and per-response usage in the transcripts. Cost after the first check is each run's reported cost times its share of weighted tokens after that point (output 5×, cache write 2×, cache read 0.1× input).

findings.title: The goal check wanted an outside review that TASK.md forbids
findings.found:
The Testing variant ends with "Don't use subagents or workflows to debate, review, judge or audit." The goal check, which reads only the transcript, repeatedly called the builder's own evidence not independent:

- opus-xhigh tenchu2: "the transcript's only evidence for that is the agent's own tests/audit.mjs mapping"
- opus-medium rugby: "verification rests on the agent's self-written checks"
- opus-medium Killer7: "the per-feature evidence comes from tests the agent wrote rather than an independent check"

Builders saw the conflict and stopped there. opus-medium DOAX: "The one thing the review still asks for is an outside per-feature review, which TASK.md forbids, so I've stopped there". It then asked you to run /goal clear, in a run nobody watches. Opus medium Killer7, BigBuckHunterPro and cricket did the same.
findings.did: Left for you. The new goal text may avoid it, since it asks what's done rather than what's proven. See Your call.
findings.check: Final goal reasons of the 73 unmet builds (`goalReason`), and the builders' last messages in their transcripts.

findings.title: Plans hard-code the plan run's own file names, and 67 builders had to translate them
findings.found: The planner's TASK.md names its files after the plan run (`…-claude-opus-5-5-max-20261103-174728`), and 23 of 25 plans copy those names into PLAN.md, 91 times in all. Each builder's TASK.md has its own names. "TASK.md wins" settled it, and no build shipped under the planner's names, but 67 builders said it cost time: opus-xhigh baseball wrote that "every path in the plan had to be translated".
findings.did: Left for you: tell the planner not to write file names (Your call).
findings.check: `grep -c claude-opus-5-5-max` on every PLAN.md, and the prompt-feedback catalogue.

findings.title: The title rule pulls two ways: 10 builds drew their own, and 2 that kept the plan's were marked down
findings.found:
TASK.md's Game Title says to brainstorm 50 titles and pick one at random. Every plan had already drawn one, and 10 plans said not to draw again. STAGE.md said to use the plan's title, "where they disagree, TASK.md wins".

- 10 of 96 builds drew their own title: Haiku 7, Opus medium 2 and Opus xhigh 1. The same game then exists under two names, like BASKETBLAM, BASHKETBALL and ZONEFIRE.
- Two Sonnet builds kept the plan's title as told, and the goal check counted it against them: SmashTV ("did not run a draw of my own") and american-football.

21 runs named it confusing. The new build stage ("Build the game PLAN.md describes. Take your file names and what to hand in from TASK.md") doesn't settle it, because TASK.md still asks for a draw.
findings.did: Insights → Expectations now checks that the builds of one plan keep its title (DASH-2). The rule itself is your call.
findings.check: Each build's title from its exit interview (`aiHub.name`), compared with PLAN.md's first heading.

findings.title: Haiku builds a slice and says so: 0 of 24 goals met, first stop at 29 minutes
findings.found:
Haiku medium, all 24 builds:

- **Goal:** met by none. 20 were stopped by Claude Code, and 4 hit the 120-minute time limit (Killer7, brigandine, ice-hockey and cricket). Each of those 4 still left a game and an exit interview.
- **Time and cost:** median 56 minutes and $6, $147 in all. It first tried to stop after a median of 29 minutes.
- **Scope:** it says plainly what it cut. haiku-medium summer-and-winter-olympic: "I built three events and stopped there". WipeoutHD left out "season, academy, versus, replay, ghosts, Overclock, Snipeout, hot lap, AI Hub multiplayer, voices".
- **The absent user:** 4 runs stopped to ask you to choose a scope.
- **Titles:** it re-drew 7 of the 10 changed titles (PLAN-3).
- **Testing:** thin. tenchu2 found 0 game bugs, and its checks "do not cover a full playthrough". cricket says "no bot plays the whole five-chapter story". Two exit interviews have their answers in the wrong slots (TimeCrisis3, Gauntlet).
- **Players:** 5 of 24 builds report 1 player only, which suggests the hub multiplayer wasn't built.
findings.did: Left for you (Your call). The time limit for Haiku and Sonnet is 180 minutes now.
findings.check: result.json, goal reasons, exit interviews and transcripts of the 24 Haiku builds.

findings.title: Sonnet finishes cheaply but passes no checks: 2 of 24 goals, and rounded self-reports
findings.found:
Sonnet medium, all 24 builds:

- **Goal and cost:** met 2. Median 56 minutes and $10, $275 in all, which is $138 per goal met.
- **Its own view:** every one of its 24 runs said the plan was too big for one session.
- **Titles:** it kept the plan's title in all 24.
- **Goal checks:** it re-checked the most, a median of 21 times, 83% of them within a minute of the one before.
- **Its numbers look rounded.** 13 of 24 runs report exactly 3 critical issues, and 9 report "about ten" issues in all.
- **Plan items it skipped:** some runs skipped the plan's engine patches (Gauntlet skipped E1 to E8, and rugby used none). Two said everything was built (WipeoutHD, Outrun2006).
findings.did: Nothing to change.
findings.check: result.json, goal timelines, the testing and prompt catalogues.

findings.title: Opus xhigh against Opus medium: more goals met, a lower cost per goal met
findings.found:
| | Opus xhigh | Opus medium |
|---|---|---|
| Goal met | 13 of 24 | 8 of 24 |
| Same brief, only this one met it | 9 | 4 |
| Median time | 162 min | 110 min |
| Median cost | $54 | $38 |
| Total cost | $1,253 | $919 |
| Cost per goal met | $96 | $115 |
| First stop attempt (median) | 124 min | 75 min |
| Issues its testing found (median) | 33 | 25 |
| Critical issues (median) | 7 | 6 |

Both met the goal on 4 briefs, and neither did on 7. xhigh also kept working between checks (4.6 minutes apart against 0.4). Its game files are a little bigger: 1,746 KB against 1,641 KB median. Only Opus runs, at both efforts, caught the real-keyboard bugs that scripted key presses hide (12 runs, TEST-1).
findings.did: Nothing to change. At current prices, xhigh is the better buy per finished game.
findings.check: result.json for both 24-run groups, paired by brief, and the testing catalogue's per-run counts.

findings.title: The scripted playthrough is the most useful test, but headless runs that skip drawing hid real bugs
findings.found:
What the builders said about their own tests (testing catalogue, 96 runs):

- **Most helpful:** a scripted bot playthrough of the whole game (72). Next came AI-against-AI simulations (15) and the AI Hub harness (6 as the top pick, 19 mentions).
- **Least helpful:** screenshots (19), smoke checks (16), determinism checks that "never failed" (14), and unit or data checks that never failed (12).

**Screenshots found more than they got credit for.** In the 19 runs that say where each issue was found, screenshots found 236 of 621 issues (38%). Some crashes were caught only that way: haiku-medium BigBuckHunterPro's crash was "found by a screenshot … not by the Node tests, which had passed".

**Headless Node runs skip drawing, so:**

- Draw-time crashes passed the suites in 6 runs.
- Menus whose hit areas exist only after a draw broke scripted input in 9.
- Esc and pause clashed with Dev mode, or unbound keys didn't end the attract mode, in 12 Opus runs.

Determinism checks never failed, yet 10 runs report Math.random leaks or replay drift.

"Critical" is used loosely. Runs count 12 fps rendering, slow AI turns and camera framing as critical, so the Q2 numbers don't compare well across builders.
findings.did: Nothing changed. If you want, the Testing variant could ask for the scripted playthrough to run once in a real headless browser, with drawing on.
findings.check: Testing-feedback catalogue: all 384 answers read, the numbers taken out per run, and every quote checked to be verbatim. I spot-checked the medians and the Sonnet "3 critical" count myself.

findings.title: 33 test servers that agents started are still running, some since Nov 2
findings.found: Agents start `python3 -m http.server` for the AI Hub harness, but many never stop it. Claude Code runs them in their own session, so stopping the agent doesn't stop them. 33 are still listening, from Nov 2 to Nov 4 runs. haiku-medium basketball (Zonefire) left 7 and american-football 4. Three serve folders in /tmp, and two serve folders that have been deleted. Each uses a little memory and a port.
findings.did:
Nothing stopped; they're your processes. To see them:

`ps -eo pid,lstart,args | grep "[h]ttp.server"`

To stop them all:

`pkill -f "python3.* -m http.server"`

Make sure no server of your own is in that list first. A runner change could stop whatever is still running in a run's folder after its agent exits.
findings.check: `pgrep -f http.server`, each process's working folder from `/proc/<pid>/cwd`, and its start time.

findings.title: Headless play is what builders liked most, and also where they lost the most time
findings.found:
79 builders named headless play (`game.advance`, `game.debug`) as what they liked most. The friction around it:

- **Scene switches don't take effect at once.** `game.go` fades, so the old scene is still current (21 runs). Timers die on every scene change, including the first (10). A `game.go` made before boot finishes is quietly replaced (10).
- **`E.store` keeps nothing** where storage is blocked, and it has no in-memory fallback (16).
- **Draw never runs headless** (13), so E.Menu's click targets exist only after a draw. Draw-time crashes passed the Node suites in 6 runs (TEST-1).

Builders asked for an instant `game.go` in tests, a memory store, and a mode that runs draw headless.
findings.did: Nothing here: it's for the engine repo.
findings.check: Engine-feedback catalogue: "Did you get stuck" and "hardest part" answers.

findings.title: No perspective camera in the handoff engine, and its 3D add-on is hard to find
findings.found:
The top single request (13 runs) was a perspective, first-person or telephoto camera.

- All 4 Big Buck Hunter and all 4 Time Crisis builders wrote their own perspective renderer.
- Three Time Crisis builders said the handoff "has no 3D engine".
- Yet all 16 builders of the four 3D plans used World3D. That's the repo's 3D add-on, with three.js 0.182 and Rapier 0.19.3 from a CDN, kept outside `dist/handoff`. opus-medium WipeoutHD: "the add-on that can lives outside that folder".
- World3D's track and ball vehicle can't carry a racer: all 4 WipeoutHD and 3 of 4 TrackMania builders wrote their own track physics.
- Racing tracks (a ribbon track with loops, a branching road) were asked for 12 times.
findings.did: Nothing here. A line in the handoff's README pointing to the 3D add-on would have saved the Time Crisis and Big Buck builders a renderer each.
findings.check: Engine and planner catalogues.

findings.title: 38 specific engine bugs that builders described, 15 of them found only by Opus xhigh
findings.found:
Reported by the builders (I didn't reproduce them):

- **Input**
  - A scripted tap sets the last device to touch.
  - `halfKeys` gives two menu actions the same key.
  - Pad codes are released every tick when no pad is connected.
  - `feed('move')` doesn't update `mouse.t`, which menus use for hover.
  - `Input.use()` drops held keys.
  - A tap releases a hold on the same action.
- **Rigs**
  - `rig.update` with `vx` but no `vy` gives a permanent NaN walk phase.
  - `Math.random` in the constructor and in blinking breaks determinism.
- **Views**
  - E.View rounding puts rigs up to 7 px off their hit zones.
  - Sprites scale by zoom alone, while geometry scales by view scale × zoom.
  - `m7.shape` ignores params and mats.
  - E.Road projects x and y with different scales, which squashes wide screens.
  - The x-ray mask uses a fixed box per item.
  - Depth sorting breaks for big geometry.
  - The chunked floor-cache trim was broken.
- **3D add-on**
  - With the cel filter on, the first-person overlay renders black.
  - Post filters render black without a GPU.
  - A literal `</script>` in the header breaks single-file builds.
  - Split-screen viewports are numbered from the bottom.
  - Text planes come out mirrored.
- **Other**
  - The 0.15 s music look-ahead drops notes on laggy outputs such as Bluetooth.
  - E.Arcade reads only player one.
  - A hit-stop timer leaves `timeScale` changed across scenes.
  - FlowField keeps the old map and ignores `map.solid`.
  - E.hex returns arrays that the px helpers reject.

Silent failures come up again and again: rgb() colours draw magenta, a scene field named `view` is replaced, a `camera()` method overrides the option, and mocap clips never play. Undocumented argument orders and return shapes cost 36 runs; for example, `mouseGround` returns `[x, y]`, which made a camera NaN.

TV readability (36 runs): E.Menu is fixed at scale 1 with no scrolling, the HTML Shell uses 14 px text, and E.Dialog has no width option.

findings.title: All 96 games start headless without an error; 2 attract modes throw on every frame, and 5 games miss the touch notice
findings.found:
I loaded each game's .html from `file://` in headless Chromium (software WebGL), first at 1280×720 and then on a 390×844 touch phone. No input for 16 seconds, then Enter twice.

- **Loading:** all 96 loaded in under 2.5 s, with no uncaught errors, and every CDN library loaded.
- **Attract modes that throw on every frame.** The engine catches it and logs `error in draw (scene "attract")`. Neither builder's tests caught it.
  - haiku-medium basketball (Zonefire): "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'sky')" in `drawCourt`. The error text also shows on screen.
  - sonnet-medium brigandine (Brigantime): "Cannot set properties of null (setting 'stage')".
- **No title screen:** haiku-medium TrackMania (Crackmania) opens straight into a tutorial dialog over an empty sky, with no title or menu, and stays there through Enter.
- **Attract mode:** with no input, 94 of 96 started an attract demo within 2 minutes. Only 47 had by 26 s and 86 by 60 s, because the games ran at 6 to 60 fps here (median 19, in software rendering), and a game whose clock advances per frame counts its 10 seconds slowly. The two that never start are the Sonnet and Haiku TrackMania builds: their opening dialog waits for a key.
- **The touch-only notice** ("Controller or keyboard required" and Settings) shows on 87 of 96.
  - It's missing in haiku-medium DOAX, Eye of the Beholder and TrackMania, and in sonnet-medium WipeoutHD and densha-de-go.
  - Two Operation Wolf builds draw their whole screen as a small 16:9 box on a portrait phone, too small to tell.
  - Two 3D builds were still showing the engine's boot log at 4.5 s.
  - In about 10 games the notice text runs off the sides of a portrait screen.
- **Enter:** it changed the screen in 95 of 96.

findings.title: Every --reparse rewrote every stamped game, only to change its stampedAt
findings.found: `stampGame` wrote the record again for every stamped game on each `--reparse` or `--stamp`, with a new `stampedAt`, even when nothing else had changed. A reparse to fill in the 64 replies would have rewritten about 460 game files of 1 to 2 MB each, for one changed line apiece, and git keeps a new copy of each.

findings.title: "Usage" asks for a figure no agent can see: 94 of 96 wrote "unknown"

findings.title: Builders weren't sure what the AI Hub requirement asks for
findings.found: 17 builders asked about the AI Hub requirement. They wanted to know which hub mode counts (shared world, ghost or parallel), whether a stand-in hub counts, and whether online play is needed for "done" when the source is single-player. The plans chose for them: 13 shared-world, 10 ghost and 1 parallel. Even so, 42 builders named the hub spec one of the prompt's strengths, and 14 praised the harness's pass/fail. Haiku had the most trouble wiring the harness: KarateChamp and OperationWolf, and SmashTV skipped it.
